title: Feelings (CCC 1762–1770)
hookLine: feelings are neither good nor bad in themselves

lines: IS A STRONG FEELING A FAILURE?
cards: "And Jesus wept." In the Douay-Rheims that's the whole verse. He's on his way to the tomb of his friend Lazarus, with Lazarus's sister Mary and the mourners, and he cries.
The Gospels show him feeling a great deal: moved with pity at a crowd, looking round with anger in a synagogue, grieved at the blindness of hearts.
In the garden the night before he dies: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death." Some people grow up thinking a truly good person wouldn't feel anger, or fear, or grief that knocks them flat.

teach.b: The Catechism's old word for this is passions. Not a hobby: feelings, emotions, movements inside a person toward something sensed as good, or away from something sensed as bad. Delight, desire, fear, anger, sadness, hope.
They're a natural part of being human, it says, a bridge between the body's senses and the mind.

teach.h: NEITHER GOOD NOR EVIL IN THEMSELVES.
teach.b: Then the sentence today hangs on: in themselves, the passions are neither good nor evil. A feeling isn't a choice yet. Anger rising when someone is mocked is not a sin.
Fear before surgery is not a sin.

teach.h: WHAT REASON AND WILL DO WITH THEM.
teach.b: What makes a feeling morally good or bad is what reason and will do with it. Anger can become a hard word or a slammed door. It can also become the courage to speak up.

The most basic passion, the Catechism says, is love, the pull toward what's good, and the others grow from it: desire for a good that's absent, joy in one that's present, fear and sadness at what threatens it.
And strong feelings don't decide how holy someone is. Some readers take comfort there: a person can pray with no feeling at all and still be praying. It doesn't ask anyone to stop feeling, either.

teach.h: MY HEART AND MY FLESH HAVE REJOICED.
teach.b: It quotes a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God." The goal is to be moved toward the good not by the will alone, but by the heart too.

how: Catholic teaching treats emotions as a natural part of human life, morally good or bad by how they are chosen and acted on; what is confessed in the sacrament of penance is what a person chose, not what they simply felt.

o: hobbies or causes a person cares deeply about
feelings, neither good nor evil in themselves
strong feelings that are sinful in themselves

games.q: what the Catechism says about feelings — tap the pairs.

s: the Catechism says strong feelings are signs of sin
it says the passions are neither good nor evil in themselves.
a feeling becomes good or bad by what reason and will do with it
the same anger can become a cruel word or the courage to speak up.
strong feelings show how holy someone is
the Catechism says strong feelings don't decide a person's holiness.

games.q: someone mocks your friend in front of you, and anger rushes up hot and fast. by the Catechism's teaching, what is the anger itself?
o: already a sin, for feeling it.
a feeling, neither good nor evil yet.
proof that you're a bad person.
games.why: the passions are neither good nor evil in themselves. what counts is what reason and will do next.

practice: Notice what's moving in you right now, not what you think you should feel: irritation, worry, boredom, tenderness, something without a name.
Give it one plain word, silently, and let it be there the way weather is weather, without arguing or scolding; if you pray, hold it out to God as it is.
If what's there is a darkness that won't lift, or you don't want to be alive, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Passions. The Catechism's word for feelings and emotions: natural, neither good nor evil in themselves, and good or bad by what reason and will do with them. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: something felt or undergone — a word Christian writers used for the passions.

carryVoice: Your line: feelings are not sins. Then comes the choosing. Back tomorrow, same hill.
